data.title: How a chainsaw clutch stops you from dying

sentences.text: If you bolt a chain straight onto the engine shaft, you have a saw that only spins.
But the engine never stops turning, so the chain whirls around the bar every second the saw is on.
At 50 miles per hour, the chain slices clean through a wooden post, so anything it touches gets cut.
So you hang the chain on a loose drum, and the engine spins free inside it, though now the chain won't move.
So you bolt heavy shoes to the shaft, and when it spins fast they fling out and grab the drum.
But now the shoes never let go, so you add a ring spring that pulls them back in and the chain rests.
The ring that holds the shoes in is called a garter spring.
At idle the spring wins, but as the engine revs, the shoes fling out, grab the drum and the chain runs.
A saw idles at about 2,700 to 3,000 rpm, and the clutch engages at about 3,900 to 4,300 rpm, so the chain waits.
But now the saw can kick up toward your face if the bar tip catches, and it kicks with the chain still racing.
So you add a brake band round the drum, and when the hand guard knocks forward, the chain stops in about 0.12 seconds on average.
But with the brake on and the engine screaming, the shoes grind against the stopped drum and glow red hot.
So you add a spring-loaded trigger that drops the engine to idle when you let go, and the shoes pull in and cool.
And a stopped chain does not mean a stopped engine.
The engine keeps turning at idle the whole time, and only the clutch lets the chain rest.
Add a cover, a front handle and a starter cord.
Congratulations, you have built a chainsaw.
